# A convex cross-direction potential and its precise limitation

Let K be a convex body in R^d, with 0 in its interior, and put
mu=1_K dx/|K|. The calculations in this note also apply to suitable
nonuniform densities; that distinction matters in the final example.

## 1. The lifted zonoid support function

Define, for u in R^d and b in R,

    Z(u,b)=integral (u dot x+b)_+ dmu(x).

This is finite, convex, and positively homogeneous in (u,b), since
each positive part has those properties. More concretely, it is the
support function of the compact convex set

    A={ integral (x,1) f(x)dmu(x): 0<=f<=1 measurable }.

Compactness follows from weak-star compactness of the unit interval
in L-infinity(mu) and continuity of the finitely many bounded moment
functionals; alternatively the same conclusion follows by taking
the closure, which leaves the support function unchanged. Convexity
of A follows by convexly combining the functions f. Pointwise
maximization, attained by f=1_{u dot x+b>=0}, proves its support
function formula. For uniform K and u nonzero the cutting plane has
mu-measure zero, so the support gradient is unique and equals

    grad Z(u,b)=(m(u,b),p(u,b)),
    m(u,b)=integral_{u dot x+b>=0} x dmu,
    p(u,b)=mu{u dot x+b>=0}.                              (1)

Thus convexity supplies exact cross-direction cyclic monotonicity:
for every closed cycle w_i=(u_i,b_i),

    sum_i grad Z(w_i) dot (w_(i+1)-w_i)<=0.                (2)

For b_i=b_j=0 its pairwise version is particularly explicit:

    (m_i-m_j) dot (u_i-u_j)
       =integral_{sign(u_i dot x) != sign(u_j dot x)}
                                      |(u_i-u_j) dot x| dmu >=0. (3)

Null boundary sets may be assigned either sign. Formula (3) follows
pointwise: on equal signs the indicator difference is zero; on
opposite signs it has the sign of (u_i-u_j) dot x.

## 2. What the section-centroid condition adds

At a proper regular cut with |u|=1, let L=K intersect u-perp and
let S=H_(d-1)(L)/|K|. The coarea differentiation formula gives

    Hess Z(u,0)=(1/|K|) integral_L
                         [ xx^T  x ] dH_(d-1)(x).
                         [  x^T  1 ]

In particular, section centroid 0 is equivalent to a vanishing mixed
block between u-variables and the offset variable:

    Hess Z(u,0)= [ M_2/|K|  0 ] .                          (4)
                [     0    S ]

There is always a null direction u in the first block because every
section point obeys u dot x=0. On its tangent hyperplane the first
block is positive definite for a proper full-dimensional section.

For clarity, (4) only requires the ordinary first shape derivative
of the cap's first moment. At a section with positive-area boundary
coincidence a trace qualification is needed; no such coincidence
occurs for proper interior sections of a full-dimensional convex
body. In local graph coordinates, differentiation of
integral (u dot x+b)_+ inserts the section measure on the second
derivative. A plane intersects the boundary of K in a set of zero
H_(d-1) measure when it passes through the interior, so dominated
convergence justifies the formula without smoothness of K.

This is a genuine convex potential involving all directions and
first and second moments. It has more information than a scalar
potential depending only on the cap fraction. Nevertheless, when
the cycle in (2) has b_i=0, the cap fractions p_i disappear from
the inequality: only m_i remain. Differentiating in offsets restores
the fractions but introduces information about neighboring cuts;
the vanishing mixed block (4) is a local, not global, decoupling.

## 3. Convex fixed-mass barycenter regions

There is a related family of genuine convex potentials. For
0<tau<1 define

    A_tau={ (1/tau) integral x f(x)dmu(x):
                     0<=f<=1, integral f dmu=tau }.

The same compactness argument shows that A_tau is compact convex.
For each nonzero u there is a unique scalar q_tau(u) such that
mu{u dot x>=q_tau(u)}=tau. Existence and uniqueness hold because
the one-dimensional marginal of uniform K has a continuous density
strictly positive in the interior of its support. The support
function of A_tau is

    h_tau(u)=(1/tau) integral_{u dot x>=q_tau(u)} u dot x dmu.

This follows by the elementary threshold exchange inequality:
for any competing f of mass tau, integrating
(u dot x-q_tau)(1_H-f)>=0 shows that the upper cap maximizes
the first moment.

At a stationary section through 0 with tau=p(u,0), the derivative
of q_tau in every tangent direction vanishes because its derivative
is the section centroid projected into that direction. Differentiating
the support gradient therefore gives, on the tangent hyperplane,

    Hess h_tau(u)=(1/(tau |K|)) integral_L xx^T dH_(d-1).   (5)

Here Hess denotes the Euclidean Hessian of the homogeneous support
function, restricted to tangent vectors. Equation (5) is positive
definite. Crucially a circuit whose cuts have different cap masses
uses different sets A_tau. Their separate convexities do not put
all those cuts on one fixed-mass support surface.

## 4. Exact insufficiency certificate without uniformity

The potential properties above, section centroid 0, and balanced
coarea-weighted normals do not by themselves force the sharp
gamma_d weighted cap inequality. The following nonuniform measure
on a convex support satisfies all of them and violates that bound
for every d>=2.

Let K be a regular d-simplex with barycenter 0 and vertices v_i,
i=0,...,d. Write lambda_i for its barycentric coordinates, and
consider the d+1 closed vertex-side caps

    H_i={lambda_i>=1/(d+1)}.

Their section centroids are 0. Their inward unit normals u_i have
sum zero and, by symmetry, equal section areas. Fix delta in (0,1)
and let a_i=(1-delta)v_i. Its barycentric coordinates are

    lambda_i(a_i)=1-delta*d/(d+1),
    lambda_j(a_i)=delta/(d+1), j!=i.

Consequently a_i is in the interior of K and in the strict interior
of H_i, while it is strictly outside every H_j with j!=i.
Choose a common radius r>0 small enough that the Euclidean balls
B_i=B(a_i,r) are in the interior of K, have those same strict sign
patterns, and are pairwise disjoint. Such an r exists because all
the finitely many relevant distances are positive. Regular simplex
symmetry permutes these equal-radius balls.

For any epsilon in (0,1) put

    mu_epsilon=epsilon Uniform(K)
                  +(1-epsilon)/(d+1) sum_i Uniform(B_i).

This measure has a positive density everywhere in the interior of
the convex support K. In a neighborhood of each cutting section,
the density is exactly epsilon/|K|, since no ball meets any section.
Thus every section has weighted centroid 0, all its normalized
coarea factors S_i are the same positive number, and equal weights
theta_i=1/(d+1) satisfy sum theta_i S_i u_i=0. All local formulas
(1)--(5), and all global convexity and cyclic monotonicity claims,
apply to this measure as well.

Yet each cap has the same fraction

    p_i=epsilon*gamma_d+(1-epsilon)/(d+1) < gamma_d.         (6)

The uniform-simplex cap fraction is gamma_d by its homothetic
vertex-cap construction. The small-ball component gives 1/(d+1)
because exactly one ball is retained by each H_i. For d>=2,
1/(d+1)<gamma_d; equivalently d^d>(d+1)^(d-1). Indeed the
binomial expansion gives (1+1/d)^(d-1)<sum_(j>=0)1/j!<3<=d
for d>=3. The series bound follows from j!>=2^(j-1) for j>=2,
strictly for j>=3. The remaining d=2 comparison is 1/3<4/9.

In d=3, taking epsilon=1/2 yields

    p_i=(27/64+1/4)/2=43/128 < 27/64.

This is not a counterexample for uniform convex-body volume, nor
for the mixed-integer conjecture. Its density is not asserted to
be log-concave. Its purpose is exact: any argument using only the
potential identities, convex support, section-centroid equations,
and balance must fail, because all those properties survive here.
A closing argument would need an additional simultaneous restriction
coming from the uniform convex body itself. No such restriction is
proved in this note.
